name: Nikhil Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the office at Calder Freight, a haulage and warehouse company with about eighty people, mostly drivers and warehouse staff. I book the delivery slots, keep the drivers' hours records, file the customs forms for the loads going abroad and chase unpaid invoices. I use AI tools every day; I set one up to read the customs paperwork and flag mistakes, and it catches things I'd miss at four o'clock on a Friday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Drivers ringing from a lay-by because a slot got moved and nobody told them. I live on my own in a one-bed above a bakery, which is great for breakfast and bad for my waistline. I'm the kind of person who tries the new thing first and reads the manual afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit let down. But fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent set of tools and people should use them, but nobody's job disappeared. At work I'd keep showing the transport manager the little things, like the tool that sorts the drivers' hours sheets. Online I'd stay out of the arguments; I don't see the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good news for me. I'm the one in the office who knows the AI tools, so a quiet AI world gets me a bit more responsibility, maybe a bit more pay. The rest of my life is steady: rent's fair, I've got about five months saved, and there are other freight offices in the area if Calder ever has a bad year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep automating small things, like getting the invoice chasing done by the system instead of me. I'd ask for a title change to office and systems coordinator at my review. And I'd keep putting £150 a month into an index fund, which is a cheap fund that tracks the whole stock market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a bit more pay. How much difference would that make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe £1,500 a year, which isn't life-changing. But it'd help me save for a deposit faster, which is the long-term plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Calder would you worry about, even in this quiet picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody much. The warehouse is busy, the drivers are always short. Maybe Joan in accounts, who still prints every email, but she's two years off retirement.

say: They're **decent tools**, but nobody's job disappeared.
I'd show the transport manager **small time-savers** and stay out of online arguments.
think: Knowing the tools gives me **more responsibility**, maybe more pay.
Fair rent, **five months saved** and nearby freight offices keep me steady.
do: Ask for the title **office and systems coordinator**.
Keep putting **£150 a month** into an index fund.
S0.quote: I'm the one in the office who knows the AI tools, so a quiet AI world gets me a bit more responsibility, maybe a bit more pay.
fieldNote: He sees a quiet AI world as **good for him**, since he knows the tools.
His **money and options** feel secure: fair rent, savings, local freight jobs.
He thinks in terms of **small automations**, not big change.

steps.text: Automate invoice chasing in the Calder office
Ask for the title office and systems coordinator
Put £150 a month into an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's more like it. That's where it gets interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every office should be using these tools by now, and the companies that wait will lose customers to the ones that don't. I'd put it more gently at work, because some of the older staff get nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the office side of Calder Freight shrinks, but I'm the person doing the shrinking. Booking, checking, chasing: I'd move all of it to software. The warehouse and the drivers are hands-on, so the business keeps going, and someone has to run the systems that run the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd pitch Calder a plan to automate slot booking and customs forms, and ask to lead it. I'd take an online course in logistics data, maybe £600, and ask the company to pay. If they said no, I'd look at the bigger freight firms in the city, which are hiring people who can do this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, honestly. A bit guilty about the excitement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when I automate the invoice chasing, that's part of what Joan does. She's retiring, so it's fine, but next time it might not be someone retiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Calder doesn't want you to lead it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then they'll buy a system from a consultant, and the consultant will need someone inside who understands it. Either way, the person who knows the tools is useful for a while.

say: Companies that **wait** will lose customers to those using the tools.
I'd say it **more gently** at work for the nervous older staff.
think: The office shrinks, but **I'm the one** doing the shrinking.
The **hands-on** warehouse and drivers keep the business going, and someone runs the systems.
do: Pitch Calder a plan to **automate booking** and customs forms.
Take a **£600 logistics data course**, ideally company-paid.
Look at **bigger freight firms** in the city if Calder says no.
feel: Mostly **excited**, a bit guilty about it.
S1.quote: The office side of Calder Freight shrinks, but I'm the person doing the shrinking.
fieldNote: He expects to **gain** from the change, which is why he stays calm.
He feels **guilt** about automating colleagues' tasks.
His backup is a move to a **bigger firm**, not a step back.

steps.text: Pitch Calder a plan to automate slot booking and customs forms
Take a logistics data course, asking Calder to pay
Apply to bigger freight firms in the city if refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a different game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses and governments need to move fast, and that people like me who use the tools should help others get ready. I'd still be positive at work, because panicking in front of the drivers helps nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the bit that made me special, setting up the AI tools, is the first thing a full AGI does by itself. So my office job's gone by 2028 too. The warehouse keeps people for about three more years until the robots come, so the hands-on side is where the time is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the operations manager to move me onto the warehouse floor as a shift supervisor, because that's people and hands-on work with three more years. I'd stop the index fund and keep cash, and I'd start selling the stuff I don't use, like the second monitor and the camera. I'd also look at moving to a cheaper flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's strange, because I'm normally the calm one when things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why supervising rather than a more technical role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a full AGI does technical roles better than me. Standing on a warehouse floor at six in the morning sorting out who's off sick and who's arguing about the forklift, that's people stuff, and it lasts a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea. If robots can do the warehouse work too, then I'd need whatever comes next, and I can't see it from here. I'd rather be honest about that.

say: Businesses and governments must **move fast**, and tool users should help others.
I'd stay **positive at work**; panicking in front of drivers helps nobody.
think: Setting up tools is the **first thing** a full AGI does itself.
The **hands-on warehouse** is where the extra three years are.
do: Ask to move to **warehouse shift supervisor**.
Stop the **index fund** and keep cash.
Sell spare gear and look for a **cheaper flat**.
S2.quote: The bit that made me special, setting up the AI tools, is the first thing a full AGI does by itself.
fieldNote: His **edge disappears** in this picture, and he says so plainly.
He uses the **robot delay**, moving to supervising warehouse shifts.

steps.text: Ask to move to warehouse shift supervisor at Calder
Stop the index fund payments and keep the cash
Sell the spare monitor and camera
Look for a cheaper flat than the one above the bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, so I get a window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window, and anyone who's good with these tools should be helping their company and their colleagues get ready in that time. I'd probably run a lunchtime session at Calder showing people what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do really well for three or four years. Every freight firm would want someone to set them up. Then around 2031 that work dries up, because the AI can do it, and I'd need to have moved somewhere else by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd lead the automation at Calder and do some paid weekend work for smaller transport firms. I'd put all the extra money into savings and the index fund, aiming for a year's expenses by 2030. And I'd start learning the warehouse side properly, like forklift and health and safety certificates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the useful kind. Like a deadline at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A year's expenses saved. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the weekend work pays like I think, about £250 a day, then yes. Living alone above a bakery is cheap if you don't count the croissants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do really well, but you're also stockpiling savings. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. I'd do well for a while, and I know it's a while. Saving is how you make a good few years last longer than they do.

say: Five years is a **window** to get companies and colleagues ready.
I'd run a **lunchtime session** at Calder on what's coming.
think: I'd **do well** for three or four years setting firms up.
Around **2031** that work dries up, and I must have moved on.
do: Lead the **automation at Calder** and do paid weekend setups.
Get **forklift and safety** certificates for the warehouse side.
feel: Anxious in a **useful** way, like a work deadline.
S3.quote: Saving is how you make a good few years last longer than they do.
fieldNote: He sees a **boom then bust** in his own skills.
He hedges deliberately with **savings and warehouse certificates**.
He accepts the **contradiction** between confidence and caution.

steps.text: Do paid weekend AI setups for small transport firms
Save towards a year's expenses by 2030
Get forklift and health and safety certificates
Lead the automation project at Calder

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for most people to change direction, if they start early and get decent help. I'd say that to my sister, who's a translator and thinks it's all far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd come out fine. Ten years is long enough to build a real career in logistics operations, and maybe move into planning the robot side of warehouses before 2039. The office job still goes earlier, maybe 2030, but I'd be gone from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd lead the automation at Calder and ask for a promotion into operations. I'd keep investing £150 a month and save for a flat deposit. And I'd tell my sister to start retraining now, not in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges. Mostly curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is your sister's job a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Translation is pure thinking work, so my sister's job is first in line on all of these. She's 31 and great at it, which makes it harder to hear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at Calder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably two or three years, then a bigger firm. Calder's good to me, but it's a small pond.

say: Ten years is **enough to change** direction with early start and help.
I'd tell my **sister** it isn't far away.
think: I'd **come out fine** with a career in logistics operations.
The office job still goes **around 2030**, but I'd have moved.
do: Lead Calder's automation and ask for **operations promotion**.
Keep **£150 a month** in the index fund and save a deposit.
Push my sister to **start retraining** now.
S4.quote: Translation is pure thinking work, so my sister's job is first in line on all of these.
fieldNote: He's **confident about himself** and worried for family.
He still dates the end of office work to **around 2030**.
His plan is a **ladder**: Calder, then a bigger firm, then robot operations.

steps.text: Ask Calder for a promotion into operations
Keep investing £150 a month and save a flat deposit
Lead the automation of the Calder office

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's the one where my head start is worth nothing. What would help is cheap, fast courses for hands-on work like warehouse supervision, and some kind of support so people can switch without losing their flat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about Joan in accounts, who has never opened an AI tool. I worry about the people who don't use the tools at all more than me, because a head start is still a start.

headlineQuote: I worry about the people who don't use the tools at all more than me, because a head start is still a start.
portrait: Nikhil, 27, runs the office at **Calder Freight**, a haulage and warehouse firm, and lives alone.
He uses **AI every day** and set up a tool to check customs forms.
In slower pictures he expects to **lead the automation** and gain from it.
In the fast AGI picture his edge vanishes, and he moves to the **warehouse floor** for the robot delay.
He's pragmatic and **saves and invests** to make good years last.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, where his head start with AI tools is worth nothing.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap, fast courses** for hands-on work like warehouse supervision.
**Support** so people can switch jobs without losing their home.
